title: Schrödinger's Code Repository: Have LLMs Learned SWE-bench or Memorized It?
authors: Silin Chen, Yufei Yang, Xiaodong Gu, Yuling Shi, Chengcheng Wan, Haibing Guan
lab: Shanghai Jiao Tong University (four authors), Xi'an Jiaotong University, East China Normal University and Shanghai Innovation Institute
date: arXiv v1 submitted 21 August 2026, the only version so far (checked 3 October 2026)

code.title: cslsolow/Schrodinger-Repo, MIT
code.note: The four transformation builders (glasses/), the bidirectional translator, a modified mini-swe-agent (swebench_mapped.py) and the list of 500 instance ids. Not released: the generated mappings, rewritten problem statements, Level 3 and 4 variant stores, the agent trajectories and the per-instance results, so no number in the paper can be recomputed from the release (checked at commit e2eef98, 24 September 2026). About 40 minutes for the README, mapper.py, manager.py and intra_file_reorder.py

takeaway: Instantiating the test repository dynamically under four behaviour-preserving transformations consistently degrades agent performance and raises interaction cost on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-QA, so part of a repository-level coding score is knowing where to look rather than knowing what to do.
takeaway_note: The database Takeaway, kept as written. Two qualifications from this page: "consistently" holds for Pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified, but on SWE-QA DeepSeek-v4-Flash moves 0.55 points and two of its levels score higher; and the evidence shows unfamiliar names cost exploration, not that the familiar ones were memorised.
verdict: Believe the direction: renaming a repository's own identifiers reliably costs agents exploration and a few points of Pass@1. Do not read it as proof of memorisation. The renamed names also lose meaning, the one control for difficulty (one model, 110 fresh tasks, 19 solved) could not have detected the drop it was meant to rule out, Gemini's 14.4 points come from the 300 most-leaked instances, two printed changes are wrong, and the released code builds Levels 1 and 3 differently from the text.

headline.k: on SWE-bench Verified with all four transformations on, across four models
headline.d: GPT-5.4-mini 46.8% to 35.6%, GPT 5.1 44.6% to 36.2%, DeepSeek-v4-Flash 72.8% to 66.8%; Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite's 14.4 is on the 300 instances with the strongest leakage evidence, not all 500

headline.k: go to navigating, searching, reading and probing rather than editing or testing
headline.d: DeepSeek-v4-Flash 46 to 100 actions per task, GPT-5.4-mini 11 to 20; input tokens rise 3.5 times for both

headline.k: on 110 SWE-rebench tasks created after GPT-5.4-mini's release
headline.d: 19 of 110 solved either way while actions rise 8%: the paper's evidence that the transformations do not make tasks harder, but a sample this size could not see the 4-point drop SWE-bench Verified would predict

resources.t: Why SWE-bench Verified no longer measures frontier coding capabilities
resources.n: The analysis the paper's motivation experiment follows; why a static 500-task set stopped discriminating.

resources.t: SWE-rebench: an automated pipeline for task collection and decontaminated evaluation of software engineering agents
resources.n: Decontamination by the calendar, the alternative this paper argues against and also its RQ4 control set.

resources.t: The SWE-Bench Illusion: When State-of-the-Art LLMs Remember Instead of Reason
resources.n: The earlier diagnostic: models name the buggy file from the issue text alone far better on SWE-bench repositories than elsewhere.

resources.t: RepoMirage: probing repository context reasoning in code agents with perturbations
resources.n: The closest prior work: fixed repository-level perturbations of SWE-bench; this paper's difference is drawing a fresh view per run.
The 100-line bash-only scaffold every run here used; worth reading to see how few tools the agent had for finding its way in a renamed repository.
The dataset row behind the paper's case study (pull request of 31 October 2019, a four-line fix); the transform tab on this page runs on its code.

kb.t: Φ-Bench: Can Large Language Models Engineer the Infrastructure That Powers Them?
kb.n: Another coding benchmark read against its released package; there too the scoring rules in the code and in the paper differ.

kb.t: HarnessDev: Can LLMs Create and Evolve Their Own Agent Harness?
kb.n: Evaluates the scaffold rather than the model; this paper holds the scaffold fixed (mini-swe-agent) and varies the repository instead.

kb.t: StateM: Reaching 95.3% Raw Accuracy, or a $15 Frontier Run, on Terminal-Bench 2.1 via Harness Scaling
kb.n: The harness rule on Topic: benchmarks: a number without its harness carries no information. This paper adds the familiarity rule beside it.

kb.t: Re-grading six physics benchmarks: most model failures were the test's fault
kb.n: The item-defect rule: part of a residual measures the benchmark, not the model. This paper says part of a score can measure familiarity.

kb.t: Repo-To-Skill: Distilling GitHub Repositories Into AI4AI Skills
kb.n: The opposite use of repository familiarity: deliberately packaging what is known about a repository so agents can use it.

kb.t: MOLE: Detecting Insider Threats in AI Agents
kb.n: A benchmark paper whose released data let this knowledge base recompute its numbers; SchrodingerRepo releases the code but not the results.

kb.t: RocketEval: Efficient Automated LLM Evaluation via Grading Checklist
kb.n: Another result decided by few items; the same error-bar question applies to RQ4's 19 solved tasks.

topics.n: Where this paper is integrated: the third sensitivity a repository-level score conceals, beside the harness rule and the item-defect rule.
Contamination, held-out controls and how much a single-run Pass@1 difference can carry.
What repository-level coding agents actually spend their actions on: finding the code, not changing it.
Exploration policy is a harness property; the paper's DeepSeek against GPT-5.4-mini contrast is a contrast of search strategies.
